title: TF-vector relevance scoring (foundational)
description: Each memory and the task description are represented as term-frequency vectors, and relevance is the cosine similarity between them. Cosine similarity is used because it measures direction rather than magnitude, so a long memory does not outrank a short relevant one just by length. This is the same math behind classic vector-space retrieval, scaled down to memory selection. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
import math
from collections import Counter
def cos(a, b):
    A, B = Counter(a.split()), Counter(b.split())
    dot = sum(A[w] * B[w] for w in A)
    return dot / (math.sqrt(sum(v*v for v in A.values())) * math.sqrt(sum(v*v for v in B.values())) + 1e-9)
print('relevant:', round(cos('speed up search indexing', 'inverted index speeds search'), 3))
print('irrelevant:', round(cos('speed up search indexing', 'bake bread recipe'), 3))

title: Task-driven query expansion (foundational)
description: The task description is expanded with synonyms from a small domain lexicon before scoring, so 'speed up' also matches memories about 'optimize' and 'accelerate'. Expansion is bounded to one hop to avoid topic drift. Expanded terms carry half weight so exact matches still outrank expanded ones. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.

title: Top-k memory ranking (foundational)
description: All memories are scored against the expanded task query and the top k are returned, with k set from the available context budget. Ranking the full store is cheap at memory scale, typically thousands of entries, and it avoids the complexity of approximate indexes. Scores ride along so downstream code can see why each memory was chosen. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
mems = [('m1', 0.91), ('m2', 0.42), ('m3', 0.77), ('m4', 0.15)]
k = 2
top = sorted(mems, key=lambda m: m[1], reverse=True)[:k]
print('selected:', top)

title: Relevance threshold filtering (foundational)
description: A minimum similarity threshold filters out memories that scored above zero only by coincidence, such as sharing the word 'the'. The threshold is calibrated per database from labeled examples of useful versus useless recalls. Anything below threshold is excluded even if the top-k quota is unfilled, because an irrelevant memory is worse than an empty slot. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
scored = [('m1', 0.91), ('m2', 0.12), ('m3', 0.55)]
TH = 0.30
kept = [m for m in scored if m[1] >= TH]
print('kept:', [m[0] for m in kept], '| dropped as noise:', [m[0] for m in scored if m[1] < TH])

t: Diversity rerank to avoid redundant memories (foundational)
title: Diversity rerank to avoid redundant memories (foundational)
description: After ranking, a maximal-marginal-relevance pass penalizes memories too similar to ones already selected, trading a little relevance for coverage. Without this step, the top-k often collapses to k near-identical variants of the same finding. The diversity weight is tuned so the first pick is pure relevance and later picks balance novelty. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
